Multiple CVEs (CVE-2021-44228, CVE-2021-45046, CVE-2021-45105, CVE-2021-44832) demonstrate that the package's default and non-default configurations can be abused for critical attacks, including exploitation through log messages, pattern layouts, and JDBCAppender configuration.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted input (e.g., HTTP header or form field) containing a JNDI lookup string to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j logs the input, triggering the JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j processes the log message or configuration, evaluates the JNDI lookup, and initiates a network request (LDAP/RMI/DNS) to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker's server responds with a malicious Java class or serialized object.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable application loads or deserializes the remote class/object, executing attacker-controlled code or leaking sensitive data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution, data exfiltration, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages containing ${jndi:...} patterns in any field or context variable
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from Java applications, especially during logging or logger initialization
Log4j pattern layouts referencing context or map variables with user input (e.g., ${ctx:...}, ${map:...})
JDBCAppender configured with external JNDI DataSource URLs in log4j2.xml or other configuration files
file_indicators: log4j2.properties or log4j2.xml with custom pattern layouts using ${ctx:...}, ${map:...}, ${sd:...}, ${env:...}, or ${main:...}
Presence of JndiLookup.class in log4j-core JARs
JDBCAppender.class in log4j-core JARs
log4j2.xml containing <DataSource jndiName="ldap://..." />
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests to untrusted or external domains from Java processes
LDAP requests with suspicious javaCodeBase or javaClassName attributes indicating remote class loading
DNS queries containing environment variable values or system properties in the subdomain
Network connections to attacker-controlled domains specified in JNDI lookups
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious ${jndi:...} patterns, including those in context or map variables. Audit log4j configuration files (log4j2.properties, log4j2.xml, YAML, JSON) for non-default pattern layouts referencing context or map variables, and for JDBCAppender DataSource elements with external JNDI URLs. Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or DNS requests from Java processes, especially those containing environment variable values or system properties. Scan JAR files for the presence of JndiLookup.class and JDBCAppender.class. Use software composition analysis (SCA) tools to identify vulnerable log4j-core versions and flag any use of JNDI in logging or JDBCAppender configurations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At build-time, the code is injected into Trading Technologies software artifacts, resulting in trojanized binaries that are distributed to downstream consumers (such as 3CX), enabling the propagation of the supply chain compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The build pipeline was compromised to insert unauthorized code into software artifacts, resulting in downstream software (including 3CXDesktopApp) being trojanized without the knowledge of the vendor or users. This is a hallmark of a supply chain attack.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build pipelines should be secure and only produce software from trusted, reviewed source code. Any modification of build artifacts by unauthorized code is a severe violation of software supply chain integrity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated build scripts are common in software development, but they should not introduce unreviewed or unauthorized code into distributed binaries. All changes should be traceable and approved.
key_indicators: Unauthorized code present in build artifacts
Unexpected changes in distributed binaries compared to source code
Downstream compromise of software consumers (e.g., 3CX) traced to upstream build tampering

package_info.why_malicious: The 3CXDesktopApp update was maliciously modified as part of a sophisticated software supply chain attack. Attackers compromised the build environment of an upstream vendor (Trading Technologies), inserted a trojan into their software, which was then consumed by 3CX, resulting in the distribution of a tampered 3CXDesktopApp update containing malware to customers. This chained compromise enabled widespread malware deployment through a trusted software channel.

attack_chain.action: Compromise Trading Technologies build pipeline to inject a trojan into software builds.
attack_chain.leads_to: Trojanized Trading Technologies software is distributed to downstream consumers, including 3CX.

attack_chain.action: 3CX consumes trojanized Trading Technologies software, resulting in compromise of the 3CX build environment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is injected into the 3CXDesktopApp update package.

attack_chain.action: 3CX distributes the tampered 3CXDesktopApp update to customers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Customers install the malicious update, resulting in malware execution on their systems.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in 3CXDesktopApp executes on customer systems, establishing network connections and potentially exfiltrating data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves remote access, data theft, or further compromise of customer environments.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network connections from 3CXDesktopApp to unrecognized domains or IPs after an update
Execution of new or modified code within 3CXDesktopApp not present in previous versions
DLL sideloading or loading of unauthorized modules by 3CXDesktopApp
Chained supply chain compromise evidenced by upstream and downstream tampering
file_indicators: Modified 3CXDesktopApp update packages containing unauthorized DLLs or code
Unexpected changes in 3CXDesktopApp binaries or associated DLLs after update
Presence of files or modules not present in official vendor releases
network_indicators: Outbound connections from 3CXDesktopApp to attacker-controlled domains or IP addresses (as identified in threat intelligence feeds)
Unusual or persistent outbound traffic patterns from 3CXDesktopApp following software updates
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or unexpected network activity from 3CXDesktopApp, especially to domains or IPs not associated with the vendor, immediately following software updates. Compare updated binaries and DLLs against known-good versions to detect unauthorized modifications. Audit build pipelines and supply chain dependencies for unauthorized changes or tampering. Use threat intelligence to identify and block known attacker infrastructure.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects sensitive browser data, such as cookies, credentials, and session tokens, then transmits this data via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in exfiltration of user authentication and session information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code aggregates sensitive browser data and sends it to an untrusted external server, a hallmark of information-stealing malware. The use of content scripts to access and exfiltrate cookies and session tokens is highly indicative of credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate extensions should not collect or transmit sensitive user data, such as cookies or credentials, to unknown domains, especially without user awareness and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Password managers or browser sync extensions may transmit encrypted data to trusted servers, but never to unverified or attacker-controlled domains.
key_indicators: Collection of browser data including cookies, credentials, and session tokens
HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled or untrusted domains
Use of content scripts to access sensitive browser information
Presence of hardcoded or dynamically generated external endpoints

package_info.why_malicious: VenomSoftX is a malicious Chrome browser extension surreptitiously installed by the ViperSoftX Windows malware. It is engineered to steal sensitive information, including cryptocurrency wallet addresses and browser data, by monitoring clipboard activity and exfiltrating credentials and session tokens to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Its primary functions are information theft and cryptocurrency hijacking, posing a significant risk to user privacy and financial assets.

attack_chain.action: ViperSoftX Windows malware infects the system and programmatically installs the VenomSoftX Chrome extension without user consent.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious extension is covertly activated in the user's browser environment.

attack_chain.action: VenomSoftX extension monitors clipboard activity for cryptocurrency addresses and scans browser context for sensitive data such as cookies and session tokens.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is harvested and prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: VenomSoftX exfiltrates clipboard contents and browser data to attacker-controlled servers via HTTP POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data and can hijack cryptocurrency transactions or compromise user accounts.

behavioral_signatures: Browser extension monitoring clipboard for cryptocurrency address patterns
Clipboard replacement with attacker-controlled wallet addresses in background scripts
Exfiltration of browser data (cookies, credentials, session tokens) to external, untrusted domains via HTTP POST
Unauthorized access to browser storage and active tab data
file_indicators: Presence of Chrome extension with obfuscated JavaScript code in the Extensions directory
Unusual Chrome extension installed without user consent, often named 'VenomSoftX' or with random identifiers
Extension manifest requesting clipboardRead, clipboardWrite, cookies, and webRequest permissions
Detection of ViperSoftX malware binaries or artifacts on the host system
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS POST requests from Chrome extension context to unknown or suspicious domains (e.g., attacker-domain.com)
Connections to domains or IPs associated with known VenomSoftX or ViperSoftX campaigns
Unusual network activity originating from browser extension processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized Chrome extension installations, especially those requesting clipboard, cookies, and webRequest permissions. Inspect extension manifests and background scripts for obfuscated code and suspicious permission sets. Analyze network traffic from browser extensions for POST requests containing sensitive data to untrusted or previously unseen domains. Correlate browser extension activity with the presence of ViperSoftX malware on the host system to identify coordinated attacks.
